extracted.intended_audience: software engineering researchers and practitioners (code reviewers, project maintainers, and tool designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study and guidance about how destructive vs. constructive criticism in software code review affects recipients' mood, motivation, and written responses, with implications for study design, tooling, and code-review norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response theme: Agree with the criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors/recipients agree with the reviewer’s comment and accept the suggested change or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used more commonly in response to constructive criticism; in the study this was the most common reaction for constructive feedback (many participants responded by agreeing). Example behavior: making the suggested change or acknowledging the validity of the critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response theme: Ask for more information
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients request clarification or elaboration from the reviewer (e.g., 'Could you please elaborate?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common across criticism types; example phrasing in study: 'Could you please elaborate? Do you mean this logic should be simpler or to be extracted to a separate method?' Note responses can be multi-themed (e.g., ask for info + disagree technically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Response theme: Disagree with the criticism on a technical level
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient rejects the review comment as technically invalid (e.g., asserting the code is correct under certain conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from study: 'The ‘instanceOf’ will only be triggered if there is no null pointer present thus this is a valid way of checking.' Occurred at similar rates for constructive and destructive criticism; majority of these responses came from men in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response theme: Disagree with the manner of discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient objects to how the feedback was written rather than its technical content (e.g., complaining about tone or civility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If you disagree with my code you’re welcome to provide constructive feedback in accordance with the code of conduct.' This response type was observed only in reaction to destructive criticism and was more common among participants with >5 years experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response theme: Acknowledge comment reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient simply confirms receipt of the comment without substantive engagement ('Will review and get in touch...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare in the study (2 of 114 responses); occurred only for constructive criticism. Represents neutral administrative acknowledgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Neutral
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses that convey neither strong positive nor negative affect; seek clarification or respond calmly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Could you please elaborate?...' In the study 58 of 114 (50.9%) responses were neutral. Neutral responses were more common to destructive criticism (43 of 58 were in response to destructive criticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Gratitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses that convey thankfulness for the feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Thanks for your feedback... I will update the pull request.' Used more commonly for constructive criticism (39 of 42 gratitude comments). In the sample, majority of gratitude responses (27 of 42) came from participants with <=5 years experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses apologizing for the problem identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Oh okay sorry, I’ll take it out.' In the study, apologies (5 of 114) were only used in response to destructive criticism; most apologetic responses came from women and less-experienced participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses expressing appreciation for the error being caught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Good catch, removed'. Rare (5 of 114); more common after constructive criticism and more often from men in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses using ironic or sarcastic language to push back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Please, enlighten me with the improvements...' Observed only in response to destructive criticism (2 of 114). Indicates escalation and negative affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written response tone: Anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses expressing annoyance or hostility toward the feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'what the heck?? wanna explain why?' Rare (2 of 114) and only in reaction to destructive criticism; signals high negative emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat: Questionnaire internal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure survey instruments have acceptable internal reliability (e.g., Cronbach’s Alpha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper measured Cronbach’s Alpha for questionnaire items (excluding open-ended questions) and reported 0.702 as 'good overall internal reliability.' Recommendation: pilot tests to improve validity and measure internal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat: Vignette realism and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using vignettes isolates variable of interest (constructive vs destructive criticism) but may not fully generalize to real-world behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations used: use real code snippets and comments, make scenarios concrete and detailed. Limitation: vignette responses reflect imagined reactions and may introduce affective forecasting bias. Recommendation: complement vignette studies with field/observational research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat mitigation: Randomize question/order effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomize the order of feedback presentation to mitigate question-order bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study randomized whether participants saw destructive or constructive criticism first. Note: order effects can still impact non-randomized items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threat mitigation: Anonymity to reduce social desirability bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anonymous questionnaires to reduce participants answering in socially desirable ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used anonymous responses to mitigate social desirability bias but acknowledges the threat remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling caution: Convenience and self-selection biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Convenience sampling and self-selection can limit representativeness; advertising channels affect sample composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study recruited via social media and developer communities; recommends advertising broadly and using purposive or respondent-driven sampling to obtain diverse and representative samples, especially across gender spectra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider confounding variables in study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and measure potential confounders that may influence perceptions of criticism (e.g., competence, education, existence of a code of conduct, sensitivity to criticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper included some confounders but notes others could be missing; recommends future work include additional factors like codes of conduct and individual sensitivity measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis caveat: consider non-linear effects and sample size
rubrics_metrics.description: Using linear ordinal logistic regression may miss non-linear relationships between variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used ordinal logistic regression with linear variables due to sample size constraints; recommends larger samples to explore potential non-linear effects with statistical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Code of conduct and public feedback norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Include guidance in project code-of-conducts about what feedback is inappropriate in public venues and mechanisms for reporting violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given transparency/public nature of many platforms, project guidelines should specify inappropriate public feedback and reporting channels; balance needed with open-source norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Tool support to detect toxic or inconsiderate comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate automated detection of toxic language (e.g., sentiment bots) and mechanisms to give feedback on code review comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Sentiment Bot and Safe Space Bot. Tools could provide reviewers awareness of how their feedback is received, but must be designed to allow safe feedback channels and to be adoptable in open source contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Feedback-on-feedback mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a safe mechanism for code authors to give feedback to reviewers about how their comments were received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many participants noted lack of feedback loop: 'I’d like such feedback.' Design must protect authors who do not feel comfortable calling out inappropriate criticism; consider privacy and adoption constraints in open source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Consider stress and time pressure as root causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize external pressures (frequent releases, stress) as potential drivers of destructive criticism and provide support to minimize stress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research shows stressed developers communicate more negatively; future work should investigate the link and projects may consider interventions to reduce stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: Account for gender and full gender spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider gender balance and include the full gender spectrum when designing studies and interpreting results because effects differ by gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study found women were less motivated after destructive criticism and more likely to view it as inappropriate. Due to low non-binary sample, authors recommend purposive or respondent-driven sampling to obtain better representation and consider gender when interpreting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical note: Subjectivity of 'specific and considerate' feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes specific and considerate feedback can be subjective, complicating reviewer guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing guidelines (e.g., Google’s code review guidelines) encourage specificity and consideration, but subjectivity remains; tooling and training should account for varying perceptions of what is considerate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research implication: investigate whether a small number of people generate most destructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore whether destructive criticism originates from a small fraction of individuals versus being widely distributed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future observational studies recommended to determine concentration of negative actors and inform targeted interventions.
